strengths: The paper proposes a coherent video-centric (holistic) reformulation of VFI, moving away from the frame-centric triplet paradigm. This is a well-motivated reframing that directly targets long-range temporal inconsistency, a genuine limitation of prior work.

The skip-concatenate sampling strategy is a novel and intuitive mechanism for mitigating exposure bias in auto-regressive generation. It is conceptually clean (resetting the generative state with a context-independent 'skip' chunk before a conditioned 'concatenate' chunk) and is supported by an ablation (Table 2) showing meaningful FVD reductions (e.g., 22.67 -> 17.05 averaged).

The system-level design for scalability is a valuable practical contribution: tiled VAE encoding with temporal non-overlapping chunks, sparse (local-in-space, global-in-time) attention, and nearest-neighbor temporal upsampling with a binary mask allow generalization to resolutions (e.g., 4K) unseen in training without retraining. The rationale and ablations (Table 3, Table 2 VAE row) support these design choices.

Quantitative results show consistent and substantial gains in FVD (the metric most aligned with temporal consistency) across all reported benchmarks (SNU-FILM 4x/8x/16x and XTest-16x), which is the central claim and is reasonably evidenced.
The implementation details are relatively thorough (optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training steps, noise schedule, ODE solver steps, sequence-parallel inference), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is questionable. The baselines (RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, BiM-VFI) are frame-centric methods designed only for adjacent-frame inputs and are run frame-by-frame over the sequence, whereas the proposed method is granted access to the entire low-frame-rate video. The proposed video-centric benchmarks are constructed in a way that structurally favors the holistic method, so the large FVD gaps partially reflect an input-access asymmetry rather than a strictly superior interpolation model. A more informative comparison would give temporal-context-capable baselines comparable access or report frame-centric parity conditions.

The most directly relevant competitors are missing from the main quantitative table: no diffusion-based VFI methods (e.g., LDMVFI, EDEN, VIDIM, MADIFF) are compared, even though they are the closest in modeling paradigm and are discussed in Related Work. This weakens the evidence that the proposed method advances the state of the art over the relevant class of approaches.

There is an inconsistency between the text claims and Table 1. The text states the method 'achieves the best scores on the SNU-FILM-hard split in both LPIPS and FVD,' but the table shows BiM-VFI attaining the best LPIPS at 8x (0.046 vs 0.045), 16x (0.074 vs 0.078), and XTest-16x (0.055 vs 0.071), with LDF-VFI only tying at 4x. The referenced benchmark names ('SNU-FILM-hard', 'SNU-FILM-extreme', 'XTest-4K') also do not match the columns reported (SNU-FILM-4x/8x/16x, XTest-16x), suggesting either missing results or imprecise reporting.

Evaluation is limited to LPIPS and FVD. While the authors justify excluding PSNR/SSIM, the absence of any pixel-level fidelity metric makes it hard to assess whether perceptual/temporal gains come at the cost of reconstruction accuracy; the ablation in Table 3 does use PSNR/L1, showing these are computable and could have been reported for the main comparison.

The claim of being 'the first to employ auto-regressive generation for VFI' is strong and not adequately substantiated; prior auto-regressive/diffusion-forcing video generation work exists, and the paper does not clearly delineate why VFI auto-regression is genuinely new rather than an adaptation of diffusion forcing to this task.

The core architecture largely assembles existing components (WAN2.1 DiT backbone, diffusion forcing, tiled VAE from diffusers, ControlNet-style conditional decoder). The principal novel algorithmic element is the skip-concatenate sampling, so the overall novelty is moderate and would benefit from deeper analysis (e.g., error-accumulation curves over sequence length rather than a single averaged FVD).

Computational cost is not compared against baselines. The method requires an ODE solver with 16 sampling steps, a fine-tuned VAE, and two 80GB GPUs for 4K inference via sequence parallelism; without runtime/memory comparisons, the practical 'efficiency' claims are not fully supported.

strengths: The paper introduces a video-centric holistic VFI paradigm with an auto-regressive diffusion transformer, which is a well-motivated departure from frame-centric triplet processing. The skip-concatenate sampling strategy is supported by Table 2, where it reduces averaged FVD from 22.67 to 17.05, evidencing mitigation of error accumulation.

The architecture combines several practical techniques for scalability: sparse local attention, tiled VAE encoding, nearest-neighbor temporal upsampling, and a conditional VAE decoder. Table 3 supports nearest-neighbor upsampling over zero padding (PSNR 30.87 vs. 28.40; LPIPS 0.006 vs. 0.011), and Figure 5 shows improved qualitative temporal consistency.

Empirical results on the proposed video-centric benchmarks are strong: LDF-VFI achieves the best FVD on SNU-FILM-4x/8x/16x and XTest-16x (e.g., 8.21, 15.01, 26.26, 51.41) and competitive LPIPS, demonstrating better long-range temporal consistency. The new SNU-FILM-entire and XTest-entire benchmarks are a useful contribution.

Ablations isolate component contributions: skip-concatenate improves FVD, conditional VAE improves LPIPS (averaged LPIPS 0.060 to 0.051), and nearest-neighbor upsampling improves VAE reconstruction. Implementation details are largely sufficient for reproducibility.

The paper addresses an important VFI limitation, namely temporal inconsistency in long sequences, and the proposed holistic video-centric formulation has clear potential utility for long-form video synthesis and high-resolution interpolation.
weaknesses: The state-of-the-art claim is weakened by the absence of comparisons with diffusion-based VFI methods discussed in related work, such as EDEN, LD-MVFI, VIDIM, LBBBDM, and MADiff. Table 1 only compares against RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, and BiM-VFI, so the critique of prior diffusion-based VFI is not empirically validated against those methods.

Key efficiency and scalability claims are not quantitatively supported. The paper claims efficient long-sequence processing and generalization to 4K without retraining, but reports no runtime, memory, or FLOPs analysis and no 4K quantitative/qualitative results. Sparse attention and tiled VAE encoding are central to these claims but are not ablated.

Some textual claims are inconsistent with the table. The paper states 'best scores on the SNU-FILM-hard split in both LPIPS and FVD,' but Table 1 shows BiM-VFI has better LPIPS on SNU-FILM-16x (0.074 vs. 0.078) and XTest-16x (0.055 vs. 0.071). The superiority claim should be framed around FVD rather than both metrics.

The comparison protocol is not fully apples-to-apples: frame-centric baselines are run frame-by-frame, while the proposed method operates on entire low-frame-rate videos and chunks. No standard pair-based VFI results are provided, and the benchmark design may favor the proposed holistic setting.

Reproducibility is limited by the incomplete 'source code is available at' statement with no URL, and the skip-concatenate sampling procedure lacks a precise algorithm/pseudocode. The exact inference schedule, context conditioning, and chunk-reset details remain less clear than desirable.

strengths: Targets a genuine and well-motivated limitation of mainstream VFI: frame-triplet/centered pipelines ignore inter-frame temporal dependencies, producing drift and motion artifacts at high upsampling factors (8×, 16×). Reframing VFI as chunk-level joint synthesis is a sensible direction.

The system integration is non-trivial and internally coherent: a Wan2.1-derived 3D DiT backbone, chunk-level 'diffusion forcing' training (independent noise per chunk latent, arbitrary-noise-level conditioning), tiled/temporally non-overlapping VAE encoding, spatially local but temporally global attention, and a ControlNet-style conditional VAE decoder. Figure 2 communicates the pipeline clearly.

The skip-concatenate sampling heuristic is simple and plausible, and Table 2 gives a quantitative signal that it helps (FVD 22.67 → 17.05 averaged, ~24.8%), with the conditional VAE giving a further LPIPS gain (0.060 → 0.051).

The method reports the best FVD on every benchmark column in Table 1 (8.21 / 15.01 / 26.26 / 51.41), which is a consistent, if metric-dependent, empirical advantage over RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, and BiM-VFI.
Qualitative comparisons (Figure 5) show visibly fewer artifacts than AMT/EMA-VFI/BiM-VFI on large-motion cases (bird wing, skateboard), and the highlighted failure regions of baselines are credible.

The paper is generally readable, with a clear statement of the two claimed limitations of prior work (frame-centric formulation; quadratic cost of full attention) and a corresponding design rationale.
weaknesses: The most relevant baselines are missing. Section 2.1 explicitly lists diffusion-based VFI (LDMVFI [11], EDEN [60], LBDDM [33], MADIFF [20], VDIM [24]) as the closest line of work, yet Table 1 contains only optical-flow/warping methods (RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, BiM-VFI). Since the paper's stated motivation is that diffusion-based VFI is frame-centric, the absence of any diffusion-VFI comparison means the central comparative claim is never tested against its own family.

The comparison protocol structurally favors the proposed method. Baselines are run frame-by-frame/recursively (e.g., to reach 16× they must chain many interpolations from adjacent frames only), while LDF-VFI conditions on the entire low-frame-rate video. The resulting gaps (e.g., RIFE LPIPS 0.110 vs. 0.078 at 16×) largely reflect information/context asymmetry and error chaining in baselines that were never designed for this regime, not a demonstrated modeling advantage. Introducing bespoke 'entire' benchmarks (SNU-FILM-entire, XTest-entire) compounds this, since the proposed method is the only one that can exploit the benchmark's added information.

Efficiency and scalability claims are never quantified. The abstract and contributions emphasize 'efficient processing of long sequences' and 'generalization to arbitrary spatial resolutions (e.g., 4K) at inference without retraining,' yet there is no parameter count, FLOPs, latency, or peak-memory table anywhere, and no 4K quantitative result. The only concrete statement is that 4K inference needs Ulysses sequence parallelism on two 80GB GPUs (Section 4.1), which is arguably a scalability *cost*, not a demonstrated efficiency benefit. For a paper whose architecture is built on a large T2V DiT, this omission is material.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is partly contradicted by the authors' own table. On LPIPS, LDF-VFI is best only at SNU-FILM-8×; RIFE is better at 4× (0.028 vs. 0.032) and BiM-VFI is better at 16× (0.074 vs. 0.078) and XTest-16× (0.055 vs. 0.071). The abstract's claim of 'superior per-frame quality' across 'challenging long-sequence benchmarks' is therefore not supported by the reported evidence.

Metric protocol is unclear and the numbers are suspicious. FVD values of 8.21–15.28 are far below the range typically reported for these benchmarks, and Section 4.3 states metrics are 'computed frame-wise and averaged over each video,' which is not the standard FVD (clip-set) protocol; the feature extractor, clip length, and aggregation are never specified. There is also a text/table mismatch: Section 4.3 claims the best scores on the 'SNU-FILM-hard split' and 'XTest-4K', but Table 1 only reports 4×/8×/16× and 'XTest-16×'. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the quantitative comparison.

Novelty is largely compositional. The DiT backbone, VAE, tiled VAE encoding (footnote 2 points to the diffusers Wan autoencoder), diffusion forcing, ControlNet-style conditional decoder, and sparse attention are all imported or lightly adapted. The only genuinely new mechanism is the skip-concatenate ordering, which is a heuristic without analysis (no argument for why an independent chunk is safe, no error-propagation measurement), and it is not ablated against the obvious alternative — generating *all* chunks independently and concatenating — which would be the natural test of whether the skip/concatenate alternation is necessary.

There is an internal tension in the 'holistic' framing. The method processes fixed-length temporal chunks (20 frames) and, per Section 3.3, applies full attention only 'within the processing window,' with the window described as 'fixed and relatively short.' This bounds the effective temporal receptive field, which sits uneasily with the claims of long-range temporal coherence and holistic whole-video modeling. The paper never measures coherence as a function of sequence length, which is precisely the property the design is meant to deliver.

Ablations are thin. Table 2 only varies AR order and VAE type, and Table 3 evaluates VAE reconstruction on *observed keyframes* only (a 4× setting, with PSNR/LPIPS/L1 and no FVD). There is no ablation of chunk length, tiling size/stride, sparse-attention window, number of Euler steps, or model scale — i.e., none of the design choices that the contribution section highlights as important are isolated.

Reproducibility is weak in practice. Training uses a Wan2.1-initialized DiT for 16k steps at batch 256 plus VAE finetuning on LAVIB with a discriminator — a compute budget unlikely to be matched in most academic settings — and the abstract's code link is a dangling placeholder ('The source code is available at').

The claim 'We are the first to employ auto-regressive generation for VFI' is unsupported and probably incorrect; recursive/sequential VFI formulations (e.g., quadratic video interpolation and its successors) predate this work, and no search or qualification is offered.

Baseline LPIPS spread (e.g., RIFE 0.028 vs. AMT 0.125 at 4×, and RIFE 0.110 at 16×) is unusually large compared to commonly reported values for these datasets, suggesting the recursive re-implementation of baselines is the dominant factor in the reported gaps. The paper does not validate its baseline harness against published numbers, which it should do before drawing SOTA conclusions.

Presentation/carelessness: references [23] and [24] are duplicates (same authors, title, venue, pages), the 'SNU-FILM-hard'/'XTest-4K' naming does not match the tables, and the abstract's code URL is empty.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel video-centric (holistic) VFI paradigm that synthesizes all frames within a temporal chunk in a single inference, directly addressing the well-motivated limitation that frame-centric triplet processing ignores inter-frame temporal dependencies and produces inconsistent interpolations.

The skip-concatenate sampling strategy is a clean, well-motivated remedy for exposure bias in AR generation; the ablation (Table 3) shows a clear FVD improvement (22.67 → 17.05 averaged) and the temporal coherence analysis in Figure 6 supports the mechanism.
Strong empirical results: LDF-VFI attains best or second-best FVD across all SNU-FILM settings (4×/8×/16×) and X4K-16×, with competitive VFIPS and FloLPIPS, indicating improved motion-aware quality.

Comprehensive ablation suite covering AR order, VAE decoder type, sparse vs. full attention, temporal chunk length, nearest-neighbor upsampling vs. zero padding, and inference-step/runtime trade-offs (Tables 3–6), which materially supports the design choices.

The sparse local attention plus tiled VAE encoding enables genuine resolution scalability (up to 4K, using USP across GPUs), and Table 5 demonstrates full attention fails to generalize to 4K while sparse attention reduces runtime substantially.
The conditional VAE decoder with multi-scale LQ feature injection is a reasonable and empirically justified addition for reconstruction fidelity (LPIPS gains in Table 3).

The introduction of video-centric benchmarks (SNU-FILM-entire, X4K-entire) fills a real evaluation gap and the decision to grant baselines access to entire low-frame-rate videos is a fair-minded gesture.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is partially problematic: frame-centric baselines (RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, BiM-VFI, EDEN) are run frame-by-frame and cannot exploit the broader temporal context that the proposed method is designed to use, so the FVD advantage is at least partly structural rather than purely attributable to modeling quality. The paper acknowledges this but does not isolate the effect.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract ('superior per-frame quality and temporal consistency') is somewhat overstated: LPIPS is not best in several settings (e.g., RIFE 0.028 vs. 0.032 at 4×; BiM-VFI comparable at 8×/16×), and VFIPS is worse than RIFE at 4× and 8×. The paper later tempers this to 'comparable,' but the abstract overstates.

Inference cost is high: Table 4 reports 16.3 s/frame at 16 steps (and 4.0 s/frame at 4 steps for X4K), versus ~1.4 s for BiM-VFI, with 4 GPUs required for 4K. This limits practical applicability and is not discussed as a limitation.

Because the evaluation benchmarks are newly introduced by the authors, direct comparability to previously published numbers is lost, and all baselines must be re-run. Details on baseline re-running (hyperparameters, tuning, whether they were adapted for the video-centric setting) are sparse, raising reproducibility concerns.

The core AR/diffusion-forcing machinery builds heavily on prior work (Chen et al. diffusion forcing, Wan2.1 backbone); the novel technical delta (skip-concatenate ordering) is comparatively modest, and its justification—that strongly conditioned VFI tolerates independent chunk generation—is asserted more than theoretically grounded.

Some methodological details are thin: the binary-mask conditioning and nearest-neighbor temporal upsampling are described only briefly; there is no analysis of how mask/upsampling errors propagate, and no failure-case analysis beyond qualitative examples.

The sparse attention comparison is run at only 6K training steps with 4 sampling steps (Table 5), which is a relatively weak basis for the strong claim that full attention 'fails to generalize' to 4K.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel video-centric, holistic formulation of VFI that directly targets a real weakness of frame-centric triplet methods: temporal inconsistency across interpolated frames. This is a meaningful paradigm shift rather than an incremental tweak.

The skip-concatenate sampling strategy is simple, well-motivated, and empirically validated: the ablation in Table 3 shows FVD improves from 22.67 (causal) to 17.05, and Figure 6 provides a quantitative temporal-discontinuity analysis (mean L1 differences across chunk boundaries) that corroborates the claim.

Strong scalability engineering: the combination of sparse local (spatial) / dense (temporal) attention, tiled VAE encoding, and USP sequence parallelism enables 4K inference. Table 5 convincingly shows full attention fails to generalize to 4K while sparse attention does, which is a concrete, non-trivial result.

Comprehensive empirical study: two newly introduced video-centric benchmarks (SNU-FILM-entire, X4K-entire) plus ablations on AR order, VAE type (conditional vs. unconditional), attention mechanism, temporal chunk length, nearest-neighbor vs. zero-padding upsampling, and sampling steps. The results are consistent across metrics and settings.

Achieves state-of-the-art FVD across all evaluated settings (4x/8x/16x and X4K-16x), with especially large gains on motion-heavy benchmarks where frame-centric baselines degrade, which supports the central claim about large-motion temporal coherence.

The conditional VAE decoder is a reasonable, ablated contribution (Table 3: LPIPS 0.060→0.051, FVD 17.05→16.49), and the nearest-neighbor upsampling study (Table 6) is a small but useful practical finding.
weaknesses: The abstract and intro claim 'superior per-frame quality,' but LPIPS is not consistently best — BiM-VFI (SNU-FILM-16x) and EDEN (X4K) beat it, and VFIPS/FloLPIPS are mixed. The fidelity claim should be softened to 'competitive per-frame quality with superior temporal consistency.'

Inference cost is substantially higher than baselines (Table 4: 3.36 s/frame at 8x vs. 0.15–1.4 s; up to 16.3 s at 4K), and this practical limitation is only lightly addressed. Since the method trades speed for temporal stability, a clearer discussion of the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff (and how it compares to diffusion baselines fairly) is warranted.

The comparison protocol is inherently asymmetric: frame-centric baselines are run frame-by-frame while being granted access to the entire low-frame-rate video. While the paper acknowledges this, it is not fully clear how much of the gain stems from the holistic formulation versus simply giving baselines broader context. A stronger control (e.g., a context-aware frame-centric baseline) would help isolate the source of improvement.

No subjective/user study is provided to support the qualitative plausibility claims in Figure 4, despite the paper's argument that pixel-wise metrics correlate poorly with human perception. This is a natural complement given the reliance on LPIPS/VFIPS/FloLPIPS.

The paper claims support for arbitrary and non-integer temporal downsampling ratios, but no non-integer ratio is actually evaluated. Additionally, the chunk-length ablation (Table A1) is done under 'similar total computation' and shows mixed LPIPS behavior, so the optimality of chunk length is not fully characterized.

Some reproducibility details are thin: the code URL is truncated in the manuscript, and key AR-inference specifics (number of chunks, how skip vs. concatenate chunks are sequenced at long horizon, memory for the 4K path) are not fully specified, which limits independent verification.

strengths: Targets a genuine limitation of frame-centric VFI (per-triplet synthesis leading to temporal inconsistency) with a coherent video-centric, chunk-based auto-regressive diffusion framework.
The skip-concatenate sampling strategy is simple and its benefit is supported by an ablation (Table 3: FVD 22.67 -> 17.05) and by the temporal-coherence analysis in Figure 6.

Reports state-of-the-art FVD across SNU-FILM (4x/8x/16x) and X4K-16x, with competitive LPIPS/VFIPS/FloLPIPS, and includes a reasonable set of ablations (AR order, VAE type, attention, chunk length, temporal upsampling).
Demonstrates scalability to 4K resolution via sparse spatio-temporal attention, tiled VAE encoding, and USP, with supporting efficiency comparisons (Tables 4 and 5).
Introduces two video-centric benchmarks (SNU-FILM-entire, X4K-entire) that allow evaluating temporal coherence over whole videos rather than isolated triplets, which could be useful to the community.
The paper is generally clearly written and the method pipeline (Figure 2) is well illustrated.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework largely adapts the pre-trained WAN2.1 backbone and combines existing ingredients (diffusion forcing [5], ControlNet-style conditional VAE decoder [62], sparse/local attention, tiled VAE encoding from [51]). The only substantially new element, skip-concatenate sampling, is a simple heuristic (periodically reset the AR context) rather than a deep methodological contribution.

The 'holistic' framing is oversold. The method is chunk-wise auto-regressive, not whole-sequence holistic modeling; the introduction itself concedes that full-sequence inference is intractable. The claimed conceptual contrast with frame-centric methods (Figure 1) is therefore weaker than presented.

The abstract claims 'superior per-frame quality,' but LPIPS is only comparable, not superior: EDEN (0.021 vs 0.032 at 4x; 0.040 vs 0.045 at 8x) and BiM-VFI (0.074 vs 0.078 at 16x) are better or equal at several settings. The real advantage is FVD; the abstract overstates the evidence.

The evaluation protocol structurally favors the proposed method: frame-centric baselines (RIFE, AMT, EMA-VFI, BiM-VFI, EDEN) are run frame-by-frame on new video-centric benchmarks that reward long-range temporal modeling. There is no comparison against other video-centric or auto-regressive/diffusion VFI approaches that operate on longer context, so the source of the FVD gains is ambiguous.

Heavy reliance on FVD as the primary evidence is questionable given its known sensitivity; there is no user study, and the temporal-coherence claim rests mainly on a mean L1 difference between adjacent frames (Figure 6), which is a weak proxy for perceptual temporal consistency.

Reproducibility gap: the abstract states 'The source code is available at' with no URL provided, and key details (model size, exact baseline inference protocol, full training data composition) are missing.

Several secondary claims are under-supported, e.g., generalization to 'arbitrary spatial resolutions ... without retraining' is only demonstrated at 4K, and the contribution of the conditional VAE decoder is modest (LPIPS improvement in Table 3), yet it is presented as a central design element.
